news.title: Still Making Headlines! What Past Root 100 Honorees Are Up To Right Now
news.text:
It’s no secret that Black politicians, athletes, leaders and entertainers honored on The Root 100 annual list always make their mark, but the story doesn’t stop there! For 17 years, The Root 100 has celebrated the Black visionaries, cultural icons and changemakers shaping conversations, breaking barriers and influencing generations. 

From award-winning legends like Misty Copeland and groundbreaking journalist Abby Phillip to cultural icons and game-changing leaders like Jasmine Crockett and Al Roker, these trailblazers continued making moves in 2026. Now, we’re checking in on where they are, celebrating the wins, the milestones and moments that keep their names in the conversation.

Abby Phillip Then

Abby Phillip joined The Root 100 in 2025, celebrating her influential journalism and contributions to conversations about politics, power and representation.

Abby Phillip Now

Abby Phillip has continued commanding the political conversation as CNN’s “NewsNight” anchor. In 2026, she also appeared at the Library of Congress National Book Festival, bringing her work on Jesse Jackson and Black political power to readers. Phillip and her husband, Marcus Richardson, welcomed their second child, son Maxwell Elias Richardson, in October following an IVF journey.

Randall Woodfin Then

Birmingham Mayor Randall Woodfin joined The Root 100 in 2018, earning recognition for his leadership and commitment to creating new opportunities for residents of one of America’s most historic Black cities.

Randall Woodfin Now

Randall Woodfin is still putting Birmingham first! In November 2025, the mayor officially began his third term, continuing his work to revitalize the city’s neighborhoods, expand educational opportunities and strengthen economic development. Through initiatives like Birmingham Promise, he’s also keeping his focus on creating pathways to college and careers for the next generation. His mission to build a stronger Birmingham is far from finished!

Misty Copeland Then

Misty Copeland joined The Root 100 celebration in 2023, honoring her groundbreaking career and lasting impact on ballet and Black representation.

Misy Copeland Now

Misty Copeland has never been content with simply breaking barriers; she’s determined to make sure others can walk through them, too. In 2026, the ballet trailblazer added a new distinction to her résumé, joining the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Board of Trustees while continuing her advocacy for greater access to dance.

Jasmine Crockett Then

Texas Rep. Jasmine Crockett hit the Root 100 red carpet in 2024, celebrating her fearless leadership and growing influence in American politics.

RELATED: PHOTOS: The Root 100 Gala Is Back! Take a Look Back at Last Year’s Best Moments

Jasmine Crockett Now

The Texas congresswoman spent 2026 keeping the pressure on Washington, championing voting rights and civil rights while continuing to challenge political power with the sharp tongue and fearless approach that have made her a force in the national conversation. With her exiting Congress come January, her future is limitless… and you can bet that The Root will be following along for the ride!

Marc Lamont Hill Then

Marc Lamont Hill brought his signature blend of journalism, scholarship and cultural commentary to The Root 100, celebrating his influence as an educator, author and outspoken voice in conversations about race, politics and social justice.

Marc Lamont Hill Now

Marc Lamont Hill is taking the conversation from the classroom to the page and the podcast studio! In 2026, the CUNY professor expanded his literary legacy with the release of “Schooling Against the Prison: Education, Imagination, and the Promise of Abolition,” examining the relationship between education and the criminal justice system… And that’s all on top of becoming a fan favorite on the “Joe Budden Podcast,” one of the biggest platforms in the U.S. Whether he’s teaching, writing or challenging the status quo, Hill isn’t slowing down.

Leslie Odom Jr. Then

Leslie Odom Jr. brought his star power to The Root 100 in 2023, celebrating his award-winning career on Broadway and beyond.

Leslie Odom Jr. Now

Some roles are career-defining. Others become part of your legacy. For Leslie Odom Jr., Aaron Burr is both. In 2026, the Tony Award winner returned to the role that helped make him a Broadway sensation, bringing his celebrated “Hamilton” performance to London’s West End and introducing a new audience to the magic.

Tamron Hall Then

Tamron Hall joined The Root 100’s celebration of Black achievement, bringing her celebrated journalism career and commitment to storytelling into the spotlight.

Tamron Hall Now

Tamron Hall continues making moves in daytime television! In September 2026, the Emmy-winning journalist returned for season eight of her nationally syndicated talk show, continuing to bring heartfelt conversations, celebrity interviews and stories that matter to audiences. She’s also preparing to share more of her personal journey in her upcoming memoir, “Bet on Yourself,” arriving in January 2027.

Nikole Hannah-Jones Then

Nikole Hannah-Jones joined The Root 100 in 2019, earning recognition for her groundbreaking investigative journalism and her work documenting the history of racial inequality in America.

Nikole Hannah-Jones Now

Nikole Hannah-Jones is continuing to shape conversations about race, history and democracy. In 2026, the Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist remains a leading voice through her work at Howard University and the legacy of her groundbreaking “1619 Project.” She’s also expanding her cultural footprint with a new venture, North Star Books + Bar, a Brooklyn bookstore and gathering space celebrating Black literature, artistry and community.

Gayle King Then

Gayle King brought her signature warmth and journalistic excellence to The Root 100, celebrating her influence as one of America’s most recognizable media voices.

Gayle King Now

Gayle King isn’t going anywhere! In 2026, the veteran journalist renewed her CBS News contract, reaffirming her place at “CBS Mornings” after 14 years on the show. She also continues her work with Oprah Daily and SiriusXM, proving there’s plenty more storytelling ahead.

Deanté Kyle Then

Deanté Kyle joined The Root 100 community of influential voices, bringing his distinctive perspective and passion for amplifying Black culture.

Deanté Kyle Now

Deanté Kyle took his “Grits & Eggs” podcast from truck-stop conversations to national recognition. He’s grown to over 612,000 followers on Instagram and 244,000 subscribers.

Kamala Harris Then

Kamala Harris has spent her career making history, from serving as California’s first Black woman attorney general to becoming the first woman, first Black American and first South Asian American vice president of the United States. Her place in The Root 100 community reflects a political career that has helped reshape American leadership.

Kamala Harris Now

Kamala Harris is continuing to make her presence felt beyond the White House. In 2026, the former vice president relaunched her political organizing platform as Headquarters, an initiative focused on engaging and mobilizing the next generation of voters and activists. She’s also returned to the campaign trail, supporting Democratic candidates ahead of the midterm elections while keeping her own political future in the spotlight. Whatever comes next, Harris is making it clear that her public service journey isn’t over.

Ledisi Then 

Ledisi took the stage at The Root 100 in 2024, bringing her powerhouse vocals and unmistakable presence to a celebration of Black excellence and cultural influence.

Ledisi is taking her talents to Broadway! In 2026, the Grammy-winning singer stepped into her first principal Broadway role as Tallulah Clarke in “Wanted,” while earning another Grammy nomination for her Dinah Washington tribute album, “For Dinah.” From music to musical theater, Ledisi continues expanding her artistic legacy.

Don Lemon Then

Don Lemon joined fellow influential journalists at The Root 100 in 2025, celebrating his career and impact on American media.

Don Lemon Now

Despite being arrested and federally charged with conspiring to violate someone’s constitutional rights and violating the FACE Act, journalist Don Lemon continues to build his independent media empire, with more than 1.25 million YouTube subscribers and over 10 million followers across platforms. He also earned a spot on the 2026 Out100 for his journalism and visibility as a Black gay media personality.

Ava Duvernay Then

Filmmaker Ava DuVernay joined The Root 100’s celebration of Black excellence, earning recognition for her groundbreaking work behind the camera and her commitment to telling stories that challenge, inspire and reshape the cultural conversation.

Ava Duvernay Now

Ava DuVernay is once again bringing history into focus. In 2026, the award-winning filmmaker unveiled “14th,” a new documentary examining the history and ongoing significance of the 14th Amendment. The project follows the legacy of her acclaimed documentary “13th,” continuing her exploration of race, justice and American history. Set to premiere on Netflix in December, “14th” marks another powerful chapter in DuVernay’s career as a filmmaker committed to stories that matter.

Kecia Lewis Then

Kecia Lewis brought decades of Broadway excellence to The Root 100, celebrating a remarkable career dedicated to storytelling and theatrical excellence.

Kecia Lewis Now

Kecia Lewis is taking her talents from one iconic production to another. Fresh off her Tony-winning run as Miss Liza Jane in “Hell’s Kitchen,” the Broadway veteran stepped into a new chapter in 2026, joining an all-star cast featuring Kerry Washington, Dominique Fishback and Kara Young in “The Whoopi Monologues” at Lincoln Center Theater. More than four decades into her career, Lewis is still finding new ways to command the stage, and audiences are taking notice.

Jamal Bryant Then

Pastor Jamal Bryant attended The Root 100 in 2025, where his leadership and commitment to empowering Black communities took center stage.

Jamal Bryant Now

Jamal Bryant took the fight for Black economic power straight to the checkout line. The Atlanta pastor helped lead the Target boycott, which began in protest of the retailer’s rollback of diversity initiatives. Bryant called the campaign a victory, pointing to its impact on corporate accountability and Black consumer power. But he’s not putting his activism on sale anytime soon! His next chapter includes building economic opportunities and generational wealth in Black communities.

Chlöe Bailey Then

Chlöe Bailey celebrated her growing musical legacy at The Root 100 in 2022, marking another milestone in her evolution as an artist.

Chlöe Bailey Now

Chlöe Bailey is making it clear that she’s not interested in being boxed into one sound, one era or one expectation. Between her “Resurrection” project with Timbaland and a holiday release of her own in 2026, the singer continued flexing her musical range and giving fans plenty of reasons to keep her on repeat.

Al Roker Then

Al Roker joined The Root 100’s celebrated lineup, bringing decades of broadcasting excellence and a legacy of service to the spotlight.

Al Roker Now 

Rain, shine or a packed morning-show schedule, Al Roker remains a familiar face Americans can count on. But the beloved broadcaster’s impact reaches well beyond the weather desk. In 2026, he marked 30 years on “TODAY” and continued his philanthropic work, earning recognition at Citymeals On Wheels’ annual Power Lunch for his commitment to giving back.

Jon Batiste Then

Jon Batiste took the stage at The Root 100 in 2023, celebrating his extraordinary musicianship and contributions to Black American culture.

Jon Batiste Now

Jon Batiste is giving the classics a distinctly Black American remix, and the results are music to our ears. In 2026, the eight-time Grammy winner released three new piano projects: “Black Mozart,” “Monk Meditations” and “Monk Movements,” reimagining the work of musical legends through his own creative lens. He also stepped behind the microphone to narrate “American Amazon,” a PBS documentary celebrating the landscapes, wildlife and cultural richness of the American South.

news.title: Who Would Be Jon Ossoff's Top Democratic Challengers if He Ran in 2028?
news.text: Democratic U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff has insisted he has no interest in running for president in 2028, but his commanding reelection in Georgia and rapid rise in national polling have intensified speculation about who could stop him if he changed his mind. Ossoff, 39, defeated Republican Representative Mike Collins by about 18 points this month in a state President Donald Trump carried by roughly 2 points in 2024. His margin, combined with significant gains among Latino voters, men, young voters and white voters without college degrees, has fueled the argument that he could assemble the kind of broad coalition Democrats will need to regain the White House. Polling has reinforced the buzz. In a closed-ended hypothetical Democratic primary matchup conducted by Emerson College after the midterms, Ossoff received 17 percent, narrowly ahead of former Vice President Kamala Harris at 16 percent, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 15 percent and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 14 percent. But a hypothetical Ossoff candidacy would face intense competition, and two University of Georgia political scientists who spoke to Newsweek pointed particularly to governors with their own records of winning difficult elections. Why Jon Ossoff Is Emerging as a 2028 Contender Ossoff's most compelling argument could be Georgia itself. Statewide exit polling showed Ossoff winning 93 percent of Black voters and about two-thirds of Latino voters while making substantial gains compared with Harris' 2024 performance among men, white voters and white voters without college degrees. He won 40 percent of white voters, compared with Harris' 28 percent two years earlier, and 29 percent of non-college-educated white voters, compared with Harris' 18 percent. The 2026 exit polling was conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of major news organizations. The comparisons are not exact because presidential and midterm electorates differ, but they illustrate the breadth of Ossoff's improvement over the party's 2024 performance. Charles S. Bullock III, distinguished university professor of public and international affairs and Richard B. Russell professor of political science at the University of Georgia, told Newsweek that Ossoff also ran roughly 4 to 5 points ahead of other Democrats seeking statewide office and deserved some credit for helping the party elect its first statewide constitutional officers in two decades. Bullock said Ossoff could point to his support for broadly popular policies, including capping monthly insulin costs at $35 and improving maternal health care, while positioning himself as a strong critic of the Trump administration. “A non-ideological candidate who talks about costs, access to healthcare, and disengagement from wars in the Middle East will be more likely to succeed, and Ossoff checks those boxes,” Bullock said. There are vulnerabilities, however. Bullock said Ossoff's questioning of U.S. aid for Israel's military campaign against Iran could appeal to younger voters while causing problems with some older voters. His Southern background and voting record could also create difficulties with the Democratic Party's liberal wing. Jamie L. Carson, athletic professor of public and international affairs in the department of political science at the University of Georgia, cautioned against assuming Ossoff's Georgia coalition would automatically translate nationally. “His victory deserves serious attention,” Carson told Newsweek. “Winning convincingly in a closely divided state demonstrates campaign strength and gives him a credible argument about reaching voters beyond the Democratic base.” But Carson noted that Ossoff was an incumbent running in an unusually favorable environment for Democrats and against a Republican closely aligned with Trump. “The question is how much of that coalition would travel beyond Georgia and survive different political conditions,” Carson said. The Biggest Challengers to an Ossoff Presidential Bid Carson identified Governors Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, Andy Beshear of Kentucky and Gavin Newsom of California as significant potential rivals, alongside Harris. Each would challenge Ossoff differently. Shapiro could make his own electability argument based on his success in Pennsylvania, one of the nation's most important presidential battlegrounds. Beshear could pose an even more direct challenge to Ossoff's crossover appeal as a Democrat who has won statewide in heavily Republican Kentucky. Newsom brings substantial national visibility and a prominent role opposing Trump, while Harris could enter with enormous name recognition, established Democratic relationships and experience as both vice president and the party's 2024 presidential nominee. The governors would also offer executive experience that Ossoff, as a senator, does not have. “Ossoff would have an appealing story to tell, but he would need to establish what distinguishes him from other Democrats who also claim they can win difficult elections and effectively challenge Republicans,” Carson said. Bullock's analysis points particularly toward candidates capable of occupying Ossoff's own political territory. “A potential winning candidate would be very similar to Ossoff, such as Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear,” Bullock said. “Gretchen Whitmer might also be a problem for an Ossoff candidacy.” That could make Beshear especially significant. Rather than challenging Ossoff primarily from the ideological left or through national celebrity, he could compete directly on one of Ossoff's central potential selling points: winning voters in territory that normally favors Republicans. Could Raphael Warnock Complicate an Ossoff Run? Ossoff could theoretically also face competition much closer to home from fellow Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock. Both Carson and Bullock said they consider a simultaneous presidential run by Georgia's two Democratic senators unlikely. Carson said the pair would compete for overlapping Georgia donors, endorsements and organizational support, even though their political styles and potential national constituencies differ. Their electoral calendars also create different incentives. Ossoff has just won another six-year Senate term, while Warnock faces reelection in 2028. If both entered the contest, Bullock said, they would split the Georgia Democratic Party. He argued that Warnock could have an advantage because Black voters make up a large share of Georgia's Democratic primary electorate and South Carolina, where Black Democrats have long wielded significant influence in the nominating process, will vote first. The Democratic voting calendar could otherwise work to Ossoff's advantage. South Carolina will be followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia, giving Black and Latino voters substantial influence in the opening contests. Those are constituencies that formed important parts of Ossoff's winning coalition in Georgia. Which Democrats Would Challenge Ossoff From a Different Lane? Early polling makes it difficult to dismiss Ocasio-Cortez, Buttigieg or Harris. Organizers have been encouraging Ocasio-Cortez to enter the race, while allies of Buttigieg have launched a grassroots effort aimed at persuading him to mount another White House campaign. But those candidates could appeal to different constituencies rather than directly challenging the electoral argument Ossoff would likely make. A progressive candidacy could attack Ossoff from the left on issues including healthcare and immigration. Ossoff has faced progressive criticism for supporting the Republican-backed Laken Riley Act and not embracing Medicare for All. Bullock, meanwhile, questioned the potential general-election appeal of two of the best-known prospective contenders. “Gavin Newsom would struggle to win Georgia or North Carolina or Texas,” he said. “Kamala Harris, if she should try a comeback, would also have difficulty succeeding on what I call the southern path to the White House.” That differs somewhat from Carson's assessment of Newsom and Harris as formidable potential primary competitors. The distinction matters: A candidate can pose a serious threat to Ossoff in the Democratic nominating contest without necessarily matching his potential argument about winning Southern or swing-state voters in November. Where the 2028 Democratic Race Stands Today For now, the biggest obstacle to an Ossoff presidential campaign may be Ossoff himself. “I have zero interest in running for president,” Ossoff said during an October Senate debate. “I'm not running for president. I'm running for reelection to the Senate.” Carson said that denial should be taken seriously, even though politicians have changed their minds about presidential campaigns before. news.title: Congress is about to have 4 times as many DSA members. Who they are
news.text:
The midterm blue wave was largely won in swing districts by moderate candidates backed by independent voters. But progressives and democratic socialists were also elected in more liberal districts across the country, adding to a growing coalition on Capitol Hill.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, and Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, and Rashida Tlaib, D-Michigan, are the only democratic socialists already on Capitol Hill. But after winning on Nov. 3, at least six members of the Democratic Socialists of America and three progressives somewhat aligned with their movement will join the House of Representatives.

While Ocasio-Cortez and Tlaib belong to the controversial Democratic Socialists of America organization, Sanders is not a member, though he identifies as a democratic socialist.

The DSA members joining the House

The DSA members headed to Congress in January are Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, and Angela Gonzales-Torres of California.

Valdez, Rabb, and McKinney bring political experience, having served as state legislators. Valdez first won office in 2024 and McKinney in 2023. Rabb has the most experience, having served in the Pennsylvania House since 2017 and previously worked as a legislative aide for former Sen. Carol Moseley Braun, D-Illinois.

Avila Chevalier, Kiros and Gonzales-Torres are political newcomers who won their first bids for office, though each has experience in community advocacy and grassroots organizations in their cities.

Kiros, the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress, is the youngest at 29. Rabb, 56, is the only one over 40. The group is also racially and ethnically diverse, with Black, Dominican, Ethiopian, Puerto Rican, and Mexican backgrounds represented.

Avila Chevalier and Kiros both drew national attention during their campaigns for their outspoken advocacy for Palestinians. In June, CNN's investigative KFile team reported that Avila Chevalier had deleted social media posts calling for abolishing police and prisons and one post that directed explicit language toward former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Another incoming progressive House member is New York's Brad Lander, who voted for Jeffries as leader. He was previously a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, but left the organization after it promoted a rally in New York City days after the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack in Israel, at which some participants defended the attack. Avila Chevalier attended the same rally.

Midterm elections: From LA to NYC, democratic socialists move on City Hall

None of those seven members flipped any of the Democrats' 45 new seats. Instead, they come from seats already held by Democrats, some ousting current members in the primaries and others running in retired members' seats.

Ohio's Brian Poindexter, an ironworker who campaigned as a working-class populist, will join the House of Representatives after beating scandal-tarred Republican Rep. Max Miller. Poindexter was endorsed by the Congressional Progressive Caucus and Sanders, but he has called himself a capitalist and also had an endorsement from the moderate Blue Dog Democratic group.

There are many other progressive Democrats in the House, including Reps. Pramila Jayapal from Washington, Ro Khanna of California, Greg Casar from Texas, Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, and Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts who do not belong to the DSA or identify as socialists.

Tensions with Jeffries

Seven incoming progressive and democratic socialist representatives-elect issued a joint statement Nov. 18 opposing the selection of Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries as the next speaker of the House, saying they were not convinced he would champion their agenda.

"Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues. We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations," Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Frederick Haynes, Kiros, McKinney, Rabb and Valdez wrote.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no," they wrote.

Hamawy from New Jersey and Haynes from Texas are both progressive member-elects who joined the Nov. 18 statement, but neither identify as democratic socialists. Rep.-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, viewed as an anti-establishment progressive, voted against Jeffries after saying he got threats from top Democrats if he didn't back the party leader.

The announcement follows years of tension between Jeffries and DSA activists in his own backyard. At Avila Chevalier's and Valdez's victory parties on the night of New York's June primary, crowds chanted "you're next" at Jeffries' image on TV screens, meaning the Brooklyn representative could face a primary challenge in 2028.

Jeffries ultimately won the vote among Democratic caucus members by a huge margin, 251-11. With a few races still uncalled or headed to runoffs, USA TODAY's most recent election results put Democrats with at least 258 seats and Republicans at 174, giving Democrats the numbers to pass legislation even without the more progressive faction.

But in some cases, moderate Democrats may defect and leave Jeffries with a narrow enough margin that he needs to keep the left wing of his caucus on board.

An urban phenomenon

Democratic socialism is spreading in major cities. New York City and Seattle elected democratic socialist mayors in 2025, and Los Angeles and Washington, DC, joined them in 2026.

The slate of DSA members represents largely urban areas. Ocasio-Cortez, Avila Chevalier, and Valdez all represent New York City districts. Rabb's Pennsylvania district is in Philadelphia, Gonzales-Torres will represent a Los Angeles district, and Kiros' Colorado district is based in the heart of Denver. McKinney will represent parts of Detroit, while Tlaib represents a neighboring district that also includes parts of the city.

Lander's district is also in New York City, while Hamawy's New Jersey district includes Trenton. Haynes won in Rep. Jasmine Crockett's Texas district, which is anchored in Dallas, after she lost a primary bid for the U.S. Senate. Omar represents Minneapolis, and Jayapal's Washington district includes most of Seattle.

In Ohio, Poindexter won in the state's 7th Congressional District that includes Cleveland suburbs, and Leonard's district includes parts of Columbus.

According to the DSA's election night tracker, the organization's endorsed candidates and ballot proposals had 176 wins to 118 losses across federal, state, and local offices. The wins spanned the country, and statewide office winners came from cities like Tampa, Florida, Louisville, Portland, Oregon, Tuscon, Arizona, Atlanta, and Buffalo, New York. Losses came in Sacramento, California, New Orleans, and Las Vegas.

According to NBC News exit polls from the midterms, 18% of all voters identify as democratic socialists.

In statewide elections, the democratic socialist faction did not win any general elections, despite some impressive performances in primaries. State Rep. Angie Nixon, a DSA member, lost in Florida's Senate race by almost 3 percentage points after her upset primary win over Alex Vindman. She got 50,000 fewer votes than David Jolly, the moderate Democratic nominee for Florida governor.

Earlier in the season, state Rep. Francesca Hong, also a DSA member, narrowly lost in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary after leading in the polls.

In Michigan and Illinois, Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Juliana Stratton won their primaries, after being seen as more progressive candidates, and ultimately won in the general election. Neither El-Sayed nor Stratton, though, identify as democratic socialists.

Sanders will remain the sole democratic socialist in the Senate.

news.title: Go Local Or Go Home: Can Dems Take ‘State by State’ Doctrine Into 2028?
news.text: The summer of 2025 was rough for Democrats in Washington. Relegated to the minority in both chambers of Congress, they watched, relatively powerless, as President Donald Trump upended longstanding norms. Coming off the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Trump and Republicans appeared intent on flexing further muscle over the left by ordering a redistricting effort in Texas aimed at bolstering their congressional majority. Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries railed against it, but there was little he could do. Democratic California Governor Gavin Newsom, however, offered some pushback. Newsom directed the California legislature to redraw its own maps with Prop 50. The move worked. Democrats flipped all five House seats targeted under the effort, and other Democratic governors and their state legislatures followed suit, helping Democrats to clinch at least 258 House seats, the most they’ve held since 1992. Now that Democrats have clawed back control, however, will their donors continue to see value in investing in state government? “Things like redistricting and judicial appointments and that kind of long-term power building have really been enlightening for Democrats [this cycle],” Meghan Meehan-Draper, executive director of the Democratic Governors Association, told Newsweek. “When you elect a Democratic governor, you’re not just getting someone who's going to do good policy, you’re also electing someone who’s going to build their state party.” That argument was not lost on Democratic donors this cycle as the DGA posted record fundraising numbers on its way to winning 30 governorships, a number not seen by the party since 1993. Democrats last held a majority of America’s governorships in 2010, and during President Barack Obama first midterms, were whipped at the ballot box by what the president called a "shellacking" that caused the left's state power to be decimated. Many Democrats have long viewed Washington as the primary answer to America’s problems and have directed fundraising dollars accordingly, sometimes to their detriment. From Amy McGrath’s $90 million Kentucky Senate loss to Republican Mitch McConnell to Jaime Harrison’s $132 million South Carolina blowout loss to Lindsey Graham, Democrats have a history of spending big on federal power grabs only to come up short and be left wondering how that money could have influenced change elsewhere. This cycle proved different as nine Senate seat flips and 48 House flips coincided with six governor mansion flips and six state legislature flips. But those like Meehan-Draper who work in state politics say the fundraising disparity between federal and state races remains an issue. They also argue that the secret to winning those federal contests in the first place rests on an increased commitment from Democrats in amplifying their stateside political efforts. “Our rationale of investing in all 57 state parties so they can do year-round organizing is so that they are constantly connected to the issues, the voters, and the candidates year-round,” Jane Kleeb, president of the Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), told Newsweek. “When we invest in just battleground states and ‘outside infrastructure’—like PACs and independent expenditures—that parachute in and focuses our resources at the national level with more consultants, we lose elections.” As ASDC president, Kleeb was a leading part of the effort undertaken by Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin to push national resources toward state parties, an effort that marked a departure from the DNC’s strategy during Obama’s time in office. Kleeb, who served as executive director of the Young Democrats of America from 2004 to 2007, said during the reelection campaign of President George W. Bush that Democratic operatives began advising donors that “state parties and the DNC were ineffective, outdated organizations.” She said they argued for more outside national infrastructure and a greater focus on battleground states, saying such efforts would concentrate both resources and messaging and yield wins. Under DNC Chair Howard Dean, who served in the position from 2005 to 2009, the DNC remained influential, as Dean’s 50-state investment strategy helped deliver electoral wins similar to the success seen this cycle. However, in 2008, Dean was replaced by now Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia who was tasked with integrating Obama’s campaign apparatus, Organizing for America, into the DNC’s fold. State party funding declined, and in the 2010 midterms, Democrats lost six Senate seats, 63 House seats, six governorships, and 11 legislatures. Kleeb said the problem is that the party became too “top-heavy” and there weren’t enough people meeting voters on the ground where they’re at, fueling perceptions of the party being out of touch with regular Americans. Despite that, the desire to concentrate messaging at the top surfaced again following Vice President Kamala Harris’ loss to Trump. “There was this big mantra coming out of the 2024 election cycle that the Democratic brand is toxic and that we needed a ‘national message,’” Kleeb said. “Every room we went into with donors or operatives or think tank people, they kept on drilling myself and Chair Martin on ‘what is the message?’ Chair Martin and I kept on saying this is not about a national message; this is about each state’s candidate developing a message that resonates with them and their experience, but also what is facing their state and local communities. That really ruffled some feathers.” Martin’s DNC was criticized for its investments, yet the 2026 election surpassed the 2006 election in its number of gains. However, analysis suggested that while most elected offices—up and down the ticket—saw Democratic gains ranging from 19 percent to 33 percent, the number of state senate seats flipped this cycle was an outlier, with Democrats seeing just an 11 percent gain in that type of office. Democrats flipped 20 percent of state house seats, but the lower share of state senate seats proved somewhat costly. Republicans maintain narrow majorities in the Georgia, North Carolina, and Texas state senates, preventing Democratic trifectas and impeding their agenda. Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said that while Democrats are increasingly seeing the value of these races, their party’s donor class lags behind Republicans in enthusiasm. “Republicans have done a really good job over the last decade and a half as they ramped-up Project Red Map in 2010 and really implemented the strategy of recognizing the relationship between state and federal power,” Williams told Newsweek. “Even if the national Republican donor base did not know who these state legislative candidates were, they knew the impact of having power in the states to test and move their agenda, to create the bench for future candidates, to control the redistricting process to win the majority of congressional districts, and they really came out with that strategy.” Trump’s return to the White House has no doubt been characterized by a focus on national politics within the Republican Party, as the president has positioned Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as his likely heirs apparent, drawing attention away from GOP senators and governors. In turn, the GOP has seen a concentration of resources toward Trump and his aligned super PAC, MAGA Inc. It was reported in October that “of the nearly 1.5 million donors who have given on WinRed [the Republican online donor platform] this cycle, 324,000 of them—a bit over 22 percent—have given only to Trump’s groups.” Naturally, the president deployed a significant number of resources this cycle toward maintaining control of Congress, but in an unfavorable environment for the GOP, that allowed Democrats to make a push for major state-level gains. Trump will exit office in 2028, however, and Republican donors demonstrated this cycle with multimillion-dollar investments in places like Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, showing they’re eager to invest in state government, especially ahead of 2030 when the new census results will trigger Congressional redistricting. Nationally prominent governors like Newsom may have been able to draw attention to the influence of state government this cycle. However, if Democrats forget what drove their resistance in the era of Trump 2.0 and shift their focus away from state power, history could repeat itself. If 2026’s wins resembled 2006’s victories, 2030 could see a defeat akin to the losses of 2010 if Democrats forget the importance of state power.
news.summary: Having rediscovered the power of governors and state legislators, Democrats may not need a national message to win big in 2028.

news.title: Don’t Want to Cook? Enjoy a Thanksgiving Feast at One of These Black-Owned Restaurants
news.text:
When you’re in the hustle and bustle of preparing Thanksgiving meal plans, it can be easy to forget the real purpose of the holiday: to gather around the table with gratitude. Thankfully, there’s an easy way to avoid recipe mishaps with the help of these Black-owned restaurants. If you want to skip the stress (and judgment) that often comes with home cooking, try ordering catering or dine-in over the holiday weekend at one of these amazing Black-owned restaurants across the country.

Waffle Lounge Restaurant, Chicago

For a hearty breakfast in the heart of Chicago, look no further than this neighborhood spot. If you’re tempted to try the whole menu, order the waffle flight with peach cobbler, apple, strawberry and blueberry Belgian waffles, or the grit flight – a trio sampler of loaded grits, Creole shrimp and braised short rib grits.

Melba’s Restaurant, New York

The Michelin Guide-featured Harlem comfort food restaurant from Melba Wilson has a prix fixe menu with Thanksgiving classics. Diners can choose one comfortizer, an entree, two sides and a dessert for $69 per person, plus tax and gratuity.

Hen Quarter Prime, Washington, DC

Hen Quarter Prime, which serves up “Southern fare, Southern care with a hint of Southern flair” year-round, will have a Thanksgiving buffet with a carving station, traditional warm and chilled holiday feast sides and dessert for $65 per person and $25 for kids under 10.

news.title: The secret to beating Trump’s Republicans is hidden in his Kansas humiliation
news.text:
Welcome to Power Players, The i Paper’s opinion series in which our writers and experts take an in-depth look at the key figures in American politics as the US reshapes itself and the world.

• The “swamp creature” eclipsing JD Vance in the race to succeed Trump• Netanyahu’s to blame for his American nightmare – and it spells his doom• The man Trump humiliated may yet inherit his party

The last time that Kansas elected a Democrat to the Senate was in 1932, when a political wave driven by the Great Depression and the campaign of Franklin Delano Roosevelt sent George McGill back to Washington, DC.

Nearly a century later, another political tsunami swept across the United States this month, when Democratic candidates won in deep red areas of the country that hadn’t gone blue for decades. In Kansas, first-time political candidate and Methodist megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton vanquished Republican incumbent Sen Roger Marshall by five points — a shocking margin for a race no one thought would be close last year.

“How did a Democratic win in Kansas, a deeply red state, for the first time in nearly a century?” Hamilton asked his supporters during his victory speech. His answer? A war in Iran nobody wanted, tariffs pushing up prices, health insurance cuts and — above all — a desire for a politics of decency and respect.

Kansas has long been seen as unfavorable territory for Democrats. Only two years ago, Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris by 16 per cent in the state, and only 25 per cent of voters are registered Democrats. But as Hamilton stressed, by 2026 the political environment had been transformed by high fuel prices, tariffs, ICE and growing opposition to the data center build-out.

The importance of Hamilton’s victory, though, goes far beyond control of the Senate or a signal of opposition to Trump. In his election, Democrats also have a model for how to win statewide elections in rural, religious America that in recent decades have turned ruby red. As other publications have declared: The Christian left is here.

Like James Talarico, the Democratic seminarian who won a senate seat for Democrats in Texas, Hamilton leaned heavily on his faith during the campaign. He’s the founder and senior pastor at the United Methodist Church of the Resurrection in the suburbs of Kansas City, and while barnstorming across the state framed his core campaign issues, such as housing, health care and energy bills, in religious terms. 

Hamilton was the ideal choice for a state where 70 per cent of people identify as Christians, and nearly 40 per cent attend religious services at least once a month, according to Pew Research. That’s above America’s average. His campaign distributed buttons that said “decency is on the ballot,” and tried to create a sharp contrast with Marshall, who had sued hundreds of former patients for unpaid medical bills. 

Trump’s immigration politics were also important to Hamilton’s success. Latino voters are the majority in three counties in western Kansas known as the Golden Triangle of Meat Packaging. The areas have traditionally voted Republican, but in the wake of immigration raids in those areas in the months before the campaign, the region turned hard toward Democrats. Ford County is 59 per cent Latino, and swung by a whopping 39 per cent points toward Hamilton in this year’s elections compared to 2024.

Data centers were a final piece of the puzzle. When I was traveling through rural Kansas this summer, I saw that many residents had put out yard signs opposing more development. Hamilton campaigned hard on pinning Marshall and the Republican Party to data centers.

But taking the longer historical view of Kansas politics, perhaps it’s not such a surprise that Hamilton and Democrats were able to break through in the Sunflower State. After all, Kansas has a long-restrained populist left streak.

Kansas was ground-zero for the Populist Party and a broader rural agricultural revolt against moneyed interests during the first Gilded Age in the late 19th century, when robber barons made killings off railroads and oil. Barnstorming “prairie populist” leaders like Mary Elizabeth Lease and later Democratic presidential candidate William Jennings Bryan took their economically progressive, religiously-grounded message to farmers across America’s vast rural areas, fighting for ideas like the income tax and the end of tariffs.

In some ways, Hamilton campaigned in similar fashion, reaching back into the history books to show how a politics rooted in economic interests, morality and “decency” could win again in America’s heartland. 

Just because Hamilton was against Trump’s policies on the campaign trail doesn’t mean he’ll be a partisan player against the president. During the campaign, Hamilton emphasised that he was an “independent-minded Democrat,” and told reporters that he wouldn’t support Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer for Senate leadership.

Instead, he said that he would aim to work with Republicans, and make the other Senator from Kansas, the Republican Jerry Moran, his “best friend” in the chamber. Rather than persecuting Trump, it’s most likely Hamilton will focus his energies on the pocketbook issues like high energy costs, tariffs and data centers.

But lawmaking in Washington will only be a part of Hamilton’s influence on the Democratic Party — and his leverage to damage Trump’s Maga movement. Trump has long thrived in the rural areas where Hamilton came out on top. Now Hamilton, along with other Democrats who won in Texas, Iowa and maybe even Alaska, are showing the party how they can win with rural and religious voters who have historically voted Republican.

That’s priceless for the party. Winning in the rural heartland is the path to creating a durable Democratic supermajority in Congress that goes far-beyond one election cycle — and will be key if Democrats want to pass ambitious policies under a possible presidency in 2028.

Hamilton is no Lease or Bryan, but his victory signals that a new brand of rural, Christian left politics is well and alive in America. The question for Democrats now, however, is if and how they’ll integrate the 21st century’s brand of prairie populism into their national platform — or if Hamilton and other rural Democrats will still be on the outs in a party led by city-slickers. The answer to that question will define the 2028 Democratic presidential campaign and the future of American politics.

news.title: How Democrats are gaming out the timing of their 2028 bids: From the Politics Desk
news.text: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki explores when we might see Democratic presidential contenders launch their campaigns. Plus, Sahil Kapur interviews DSCC Chair Kirsten Gillibrand about the 2028 Senate map. Programming note: We are taking a holiday break the rest of the week and will be back in your inbox on Monday. Have a happy Thanksgiving! — Adam Wollner How Democrats are gaming out the timing of their 2028 bids Analysis by Natasha Korecki Now that the midterm elections are all of three weeks behind us, Democratic White House hopefuls can get real about their 2028 campaigns. With that comes one of the first big decisions they’ll need to make: exactly when to enter the race. Jump in early and face the harsh national spotlight and a possibility of burning through cash too soon. Wait too long and risk getting left behind in what’s expected to be a crowded field. We talked to advisers to potential candidates, donors and outside strategists who laid out the major considerations that go into deciding the right moment to officially announce a campaign for president. Here are some of the key factors to keep an eye on. A mad rush in two phases: Several strategists said to expect to see two main phases of rollouts (with the potential of it starting even before the end of the year). The first is in January, after the new party superstars in Congress settle in. And the second is in February and March, with the bulk of the field likely to be in place by March 31, just as the first quarter of fundraising ends. “The minute you jump in, you need to start paying people, raising money, all of those things,” a senior Democratic strategist who worked on a presidential campaign in 2020 said. “But time is also your friend in a crowded field. … You need to distinguish yourself.” Governing: Voters just re-elected Govs. Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, JB Pritzker in Illinois and Gov. Wes Moore in Maryland to four-year-terms. It’s unlikely they’d announce before their own January swearing-in ceremonies. And they might even have to clear legislative sessions and state of the state addresses from their plates first. Money: Locking down donors is vital to demonstrate fundraising strength early. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear is asking his donors to convene in December before any decision happens. Some potential contenders, like Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, are already sitting on a pile of cash. And while Pritzker, a notorious self-financier, is expected to fundraise for the first time, the billionaire can reliably lean on personal wealth. Staffing up: Some nascent campaigns have already locked down their hired guns, but with so many Democrats competing for talent, there are some potential contenders still wrangling over some important hires. “There are a lot of factors,” said a person working with a potential 2028 candidate. “It’s a conversation I know everybody is having.” Book releases: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg is due out with a book in January. Moore has a scheduled March release for his book. Conventional wisdom (though it isn’t always accurate) is that candidates will seek to tap into momentum from the publishing tours to then shift into campaign mode. The X factors: As we reported this week, what Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and former Vice President Kamala Harris decide to do looms particularly large over the rest of the field. Someone like Rep. Ro Khanna may want to jump in sooner rather than later to get a leg up in the progressive lane over AOC. For his part, California Gov. Gavin Newsom has said he would not run for president if Harris does — though not everyone is buying that. “When he said it, it was total bull----,” said billionaire Democratic donor John Morgan. “Put this down for my prediction: Even if she runs, he’s running.” 🔵 Related: Democrats grumble about the DNC’s plan for the 2028 primary debates, by Jonathan Allen and Natasha Korecki DSCC chair says it’s ‘definitely possible’ for Democrats to win 60 Senate seats in 2028 By Sahil Kapur Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y. is seeking another two-year term as chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee after her party flipped nine seats on its way to securing a 56-seat majority. In an interview with NBC News, Gillibrand said she’s bullish that Democrats can expand the map again in 2028, calling it “definitely possible” to capture 60 seats and win a very rare, filibuster-proof majority. “It’s on the table. There’s some easy targets that I’m very excited about — obviously, Wisconsin and North Carolina,” Gillibrand said. “But I would also suggest any state that was in play last cycle is in play this cycle. Waves tend to be two cycles long, and this is a very large blue tsunami.” If Democrats hold all their seats in 2028, their best pickup opportunities are seats in the highly competitive states of Wisconsin (held by Sen. Ron Johnson) and North Carolina (held by Sen. Ted Budd). From there the hill gets steeper, requiring victories in redder states. “I think we can put a lot of these states that we put in play last time that are exciting states like Kansas and South Carolina and Iowa,” all of which Democrats won in November, Gillibrand said. “There’s no reason why we can’t find extraordinary candidates, again, who have the right message to fight for their states to run in these very red and purple places.” Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

news.title: Nolte: Mean Girls at ‘Vanity Fair’ Rip Taylor Swift for Political Reasons
news.text:
These days, everything can be answered through a political lens because everything has been politicized by Democrats. For example: Why would the far-left Vanity Fair publish a hit piece on Taylor Swift that’s so poorly and thinly sourced, and in which her name is never used?

If you’ve read the piece, and I have, you might ask yourself another question… Why does Vanity Fair angle the article as a hit piece when even the worst behavior it alleges about Taylor Swift makes her look awesome?

It is, admittedly, a nicely composed piece and structured using the conceit of record sides. SIDE A is the myth around Taylor Swift. SIDE B is the supposed truth about Taylor Swift. This is an interesting approach when no one under 40 will get the reference.

According to Vanity Fair, Swift’s career was launched due to her own ambition which was backed by her equally ambitious parents and the fact they are wealthy. What’s more, over the course of her legendary career, Swift has feuded with fellow artists, used her relationships with various guys as recording material, and she can be equal parts shrewd and ruthless in her business dealings.

Sometimes, in both her music and business dealings, she allegedly twists the truth to make herself look more like the victim.

Sometimes she’s exceedingly generous to fellow musicians, especially women.

Sometimes, if she perceives a slight, she cuts them off entirely.

Honestly, that’s the worst Vanity Fair could find after talking to dozens of people about a woman in the public spotlight for more than 20 years. All I came away with was the impression that she’s ambitious, has no tolerance for bullshit, and doesn’t take any crap. In other words, she’s an American.

And so what if her parents have money? Do you know how many stage parents with money have wasted all that money on a talentless child?

Mommy and Daddy’s money only gets you so far.

Listen, I’m no Swiftie. I’m not even a music guy. Preferring silence, I don’t turn on the radio during long drives. But I still see Taylor Swift as an insanely talented, wildly ambitious, ridiculously successful, and slightly neurotic pop superstar who — within the context of pop superstars — is probably the healthiest example of a pop culture superstar America has seen in decades.

Yes, she’s a little self-involved. Yes, she was pretty partisan for a short time (only after being bullied into it). But look at the upside: no tattoos, no nose rings, no arrests, no sex tape, no paparazzi meltdowns. In the face of an Elvis-sized fame that began when she was still a teenager, Taylor Swift has shown remarkable poise and class. And she’s a girly-girl without any of the heavy hyper-sexualization that has defined pop music for decades.

So why is Vanity Fair straining to pretend it has uncovered damaging information about her, such as the fact she owned three pairs of Uggs in high school? (Seriously, that’s in the story.)

Well, Swift has toned down speaking out about politics — her endorsement of Kamala Harris was tepid at best. She’s also begun releasing songs about the joys of being a wife, suburban life, and having babies…

I just want you (You, you, yeah), huh
Have a couple kids, got the whole block looking like you
We tell the world to leave us the fuck alone, and they do (Ooh), wow
Got me dreaming ’bout a driveway with a basketball hoop (Hoop)
Boss up, settle down, got a wish (Wish) list (List)

And so, the Vanity Fair article is a classic (and predictable) piece of media bullying against a high-profile celebrity who’s looking like she might color outside of the accepted political and social lines. Shame on Taylor Swift for not holding concerts for Kamala Harris, for maturing and realizing not all men are evil.

What I wrote in her defense last year still stands:

For going on 20 years, Swift had been the goddess who affirmed their lonely, bitter, anti-male lifestyle. She was all about her career, all about wrist-flicking the patriarchy, all about the narcissism of self-care.
But unlike these former worshipers (who are mostly homely, bitter, and impossible to live with), Taylor Swift has options. She’s rich and beautiful, which means she has a banquet of desirable men laid out before her. She’s also smart enough to grow up and grasp the idea that being alone and childless at 40 is no way to live.

In another lyric, Swift admitted, “I like my friends cancelled.”

The fascists at Vanity Fair will never stand by and do nothing in the face of Based Taylor Swift.
news.summary:
Why does "Vanity Fair" angle an article as a hit piece when even the worst behavior it alleges about Taylor Swift makes her look awesome?

news.title: The Ghost of Limbaugh Past
news.text:
In the fall of 2006, as the war in Iraq and Afghanistan droned on, appearing to many Americans as another quagmire we'd gotten ourselves into, President George W. Bush faced an angry electorate. It was the sixth year of his presidency, and he was facing a reckoning not just with Democrats and independents, but with a sizeable chunk of his political base as well. Before dooming was cool in 2026, it was practiced by a bunch of bloggers (2006's social media influencers). The issues should sound familiar — immigration, spending, scandal, war weariness. The prophets of doom on the right grew louder with their predictions of defeat that did indeed come true. Glenn Reynolds, the Instapundit, went so far as to say the Republicans deserved to lose. In Salon, the family squabble on the right just before the midterms was too delicious for them not to print. 

“So is it over for the GOP majorities in Congress? It’s still too early to say, I guess, but when even John Hinderaker is sounding extremely gloomy, that’s certainly the way to bet. So I want to stress, for the edification of any Republican leaders who might pay attention, that this is the result of a series of unforced errors on their part. Following is a (partial) list: The Terri Schiavo affair … the Harriet Miers debacle … the Dubai Ports disaster … immigration … William Jefferson … is caught in a bribery scandal with a freezer full of cash, and Dennis Hastert backs him up … Foleygate … As I’ve said before, the Republicans deserve to lose, though alas the Democrats don’t really deserve to win, either.”

The leading voice on the right outside of government at the time was the late Rush Limbaugh. Speaking to an audience of 22 million people spread out over 600-plus stations on the EIB Network, El Rushbo reached his limit with the pessimism. 

“The term GOP ‘premortem,’ I don’t know who used it first, but a couple of other bloggers and stuff just think it’s cool … One of them is … Glenn Reynolds. What’s his place? Instant Pundit? I’m not sure, but here’s his analysis: ‘If the GOP Goes Down, It’s Because It Had It Coming’ … What kind of a fool reason is it to suggest that if the Republicans lose, it’s because they had it coming? Do Democrats have nothing coming? … Even if you believe Republicans deserve to lose, let me ask you, do you deserve to lose? Does the country deserve a cut-and-run policy in the war on terror? Do the 3,000 brave souls who have lost their lives in the war on terror deserve to have the rug pulled out from under their mission? Do they deserve that? Do you deserve higher taxes? Do you deserve increased gasoline prices? Do you deserve two years of probable investigations into so-called war crimes and potential impeachment hearings, do you deserve that? Do the people of the country deserve what we would get with a liberal Democrat triumph? You know, we look at this, there’s some people apparently look at this as a game in Washington that doesn’t affect us, and the people who go to Washington, if they screw up, well, then the hell with me with them. They deserve to lose. It’s good. They’ll learn a lesson by losing. Hey, maybe so, but how long will it be before they win it back? Never have understood this notion that you win by losing, that you win by quitting.”

It was true then, it's just as true now, and yet we still have not learned that lesson. And it's entirely probable we never will. Of the myriad of differences in policy between the political left and right in this country, one tactical advantage Democrats consistently use is they know they want to win. Even if they have sub-par candidates (Joe Biden, Kamala Harris, James Talarico, Kathy Hochul, Abdul El-Sayed, Troy Jackson, Mary Peltola, Sherrod Brown), they still come out and vote. Pacific Palisades and Altadena can burn to the ground in Los Angeles for no other reason than sheer incompetence, and it does not discourage one Democrat from pulling the lever for more of that incompetence. Why? They want their team to win. My wife is one of a very few members of a club in California — a teacher who happens to be a Republican. Many of her colleagues, who voted for exactly what is going to roll out when Xavier Becerra becomes the next incompetent governor of the Golden State, are beside themselves at the notion Democrats are promising to roll out a mileage tax. They're astounded at how unfair that is, and do not like the Big Brother aspect of how the government is going to track how many miles you drive in order to tax you. They complain, but yet they still vote Democrat. They did last month, and they will again in the next election when the tax has gone into effect. Republicans are a different sort. We don't seem to do that. There has always been at least a third of the base that finds solace and ethical satisfaction by teaching the party a lesson. They believe that by sitting it out, that'll show 'em, and maybe they'll remember who Republicans are again. The third post-election stat I've seen since November demonstrated that a few days ago.

This time, the straw that broke the GOP base back was the war against Iran. The isolationist wing sat on their hands. The red zone end of the Republican field abandoned the turf, and will not play again unless the ball comes their direction. For the next two years, the DSA will keep using the Democrat Party platform to move the ball to their red zone, and while their rhetoric doesn't exude patience, their voting practices do. They keep making incremental gains in a never-ending progressive push to the left. What remains open is the entire middle of the field between the 30's. Hugh Hewitt wrote a column for Fox News today with a bold idea for President Trump to consider in his final two years. The pith of the gist is now that the wall has been built to protect the Southern Border from invasion, take the high ground on the immigration issue once and for all by pardoning a small cohort of people here illegally that have no other criminal record and a track record of assimilation. 

Thus, President Trump is in a position to do a Nixon-to-China on illegal immigrants. There might be a "Trump-Schumer-Jeffries Regularization Act" a year down the road, a statute that should not include a general "amnesty" and cannot provide a "pathway to citizenship." news.title: JD Vance’s Wipeout Excuse Torpedoed in Brutal Reality Check
news.text:
“Our voters did show up,” the vice president wrote on X, in a claim echoed by Sen. Ted Cruz. “But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.”

But a Washington Post analysis of 13 Senate races suggests Vance got it badly wrong.

According to the Post, the biggest reason for the Democratic surge was not hordes of Trump voters defecting to the other side but Republicans failing to turn out while Democrats flooded the polls.

The findings suggest that most Democratic gains, around 70 percent, came from changes in who turned out to vote, rather than people changing their political allegiance. 

Only around 20 percent came from voters switching parties, with the rest explained by new voters and those moving away from third-party candidates.

For every 100 people who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, roughly 33 stayed home, while between one and eight crossed over to vote Democrat, depending on the state.

That finding is supported by national exit polls, which found that 7 percent of Trump voters backed Democrats, compared with just 2 percent of Kamala Harris voters who supported Republicans.

The biggest difference was how successfully each party held on to its existing supporters.

Republicans retained 64 percent of Trump’s 2024 voters across the races examined, broadly in line with historical midterm patterns. Democrats held on to 92 percent of Harris voters, far above the usual 68 to 81 percent range for the party out of power.

That suggests the Democratic wave was driven less by an extraordinary Republican revolt than by Democrats keeping their own supporters engaged while attracting some additional voters.

There were, however, several states where switching sides played a much bigger role.

Texas offered the starkest example. Trump carried the state by nearly 14 points in 2024, yet Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton for a U.S. Senate seat by 12 points.

About 8 percent of Trump’s previous supporters backed Talarico, the highest share among the states analyzed by the Post. The findings also suggested that switching was particularly common in heavily Hispanic areas.

In Hidalgo County, which is more than 90 percent Hispanic, most of the Democratic gains were attributed to former Trump voters backing Talarico.

Georgia and South Carolina also showed evidence of significant crossover voting.

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham by four points in the race for Graham’s late brother’s longtime Senate seat, representing a 22-point swing from the 2024 presidential result. Around a third of the Democratic gains came from former Trump voters.

Georgia, meanwhile, showed how powerful turnout could be. Around a third of Trump’s 2024 supporters stayed home, but Democrats were particularly successful at attracting new voters.

Some 420,000 Georgians who had not voted in 2024 turned out this year. Relative to the number of previous voters, they were about twice as common in heavily Democratic precincts as in heavily Republican ones.

However, the Democratic gains were less dramatic in parts of the North, including Michigan and Minnesota, and that is because Republicans held onto more of their voters in those states.

Democrats won both states, but their margins were smaller than the wider national swing might have suggested. Republicans held on to 72 percent of Trump’s voters in Michigan and 77 percent in Minnesota, well above the 60 percent average across the 13 states.

There was even evidence of voters moving in the opposite direction. In Michigan, about 96,000 Harris voters switched to Republicans, compared with 40,000 Trump voters who backed Democrats. 

Minnesota showed a similar pattern, with about 24,000 more Harris voters switching to Republicans than Trump voters moving to the Democrats.

news.title: EXPLAINED: France's strict rules on election campaign funding
news.text:
Presidential campaigns in France are subject to strict financing rules - and candidates who break them face serious legal consequences, up to and including jail time.

Here's how the French system works;

Spending is capped

The amount of money that candidates can spend during a presidential election is subject to strict limits.

French candidates are currently limited to a total campaign spend of €22.51 million. 

This limit covers the one-year period before the election - so for the 2027 election it started in April 2026.

All candidates can spend up to €16.85 million until the date of the first round of the election, which is April 18th, 2027.

The two top-polling candidates then go through to a second round - they're allowed to spend an additional €5.66 million in the two-week period between round one and round two.

By contrast, Kamala Harris and Donald Trump raised and spent an estimated combined total of over $5.5 billion on their 2024 US election campaigns. 

French spending caps are also significantly lower than those imposed in the UK, where nationwide general election campaign spending is limited to £34 million.

Donor limits

As well as the overall spending ceiling, there are limits on who candidates can accept money from - donations from businesses or legal entities (including lobby groups or charities) are 100 percent banned.

When it comes to donations from individuals, they are capped at €4,600 per person, so super-wealthy individuals cannot buy political influence through donations.

Cash payments are limited to €150 - and candidates are required to keep detailed records of who gives them money.

The geographical origin of donations matters too. A law passed after the 2017 election decreed that candidates could no longer borrow money from financial organisations based outside of the European Economic Area (EEA).

This meant that Marine Le Pen's January 2022 loan of more than €10 million from a bank in Hungary was legal - whereas loans from Russian banks, which her party had previously used to finance earlier campaigns, were no longer permitted.

All candidates who make it onto the ballot paper must also make a declaration disclosing their assets and wealth and declaring their financial interests and professional activities, as well as those of their spouses.

These déclarations de patrimoine are very detailed - so for example in 2022 we learned that the highest value possession of Trotskyist candidate Philippe Poutou was his car, a Peugeot 308.

Government funding

There is, however, another source of funding - the state.

All candidates on the ballot paper for round one receive €200,000 of public money to campaign.

French presidential candidates who win more than 5 percent of the vote in the first round can then receive up to €8 million in government reimbursements to cover their campaign costs. Those who win less than 5 percent only get up to €800,423 reimbursed by the state.

Candidates who make it through to the second round can have up to €10.7 million reimbursed by the state.

Campaign expenses don’t include advertising

Expenses that are eligible for state reimbursement include public meetings and rallies, campaign materials, headquarters and staff salaries. 

Candidates can also submit expenses for ‘digital campaigning’, which includes the cost of developing, hosting and maintaining official websites and mobile apps. Video and podcast production, as well as graphic content creation are also covered.

However, paid commercial ads on TV, radio, print newspapers, billboards, search engines, or sponsored social media posts during the 6 months prior to the election are strictly prohibited by law and are not, therefore, counted as expenses. 

Instead, French candidates receive free, allocated public airtime, where they promote their campaign message.

Other prohibited expenses in France include campaign bills paid directly by the candidate, a supporter or a third party; personal expenses such as clothing, medical care, cosmetics, or private living costs; parking tickets and tax penalties; and lavish private social receptions unrelated to public election meetings.

The biggest spenders usually win

Historical examples suggest that spending up to the maximum is worth it.

Emmanuel Macron beat Marine Le Pen in the second round of the 2022 presidential election, after outspending her by roughly €6.03 million - a repeat of what happened in the 2017 presidential election, when he spent €4 million more than her. 

Nicolas Sarkozy won the 2007 presidential election after outspending his rivals and Chirac won the 1995 and 2002 elections as the biggest spender.

One recent exception is the 2012 election in which Nicolas Sarkozy lost to François Hollande in the second round despite spending more money. That year, Sarkozy didn't receive any reimbursement from the state to cover campaign costs after breaching the spending limit. He was officially left with close to €23 million to cover himself.

Campaign accounts are centralised and monitored

Candidates are not allowed to directly collect donations or pay campaign expenses. Instead, all candidates on the official list must declare a campaign account, which is managed by a financial agent, which can be an individual or an electoral financing association.

This account details income, expenses, in-kind contributions, supporting documents (including invoices and examples of campaign materials such as leaflets), and transactions in the agent's bank account.

The Commission nationale des comptes de campagne et des financements politiques (CNCCFP) monitors the campaign accounts and political financing of candidates in French elections. 

Those who break the rules face heavy (albeit often delayed) penalties

If the CNCCFP finds irregularities in a candidate's campaign accounts, it can ask judicial authorities to launch an investigation.

The most famous example of someone who has fallen foul of this system is former president Nicolas Sarkozy.

In 2021, a court sentenced Sarkozy to one year in prison (later reduced to six months with an electronic tag, which a judge waived in May 2026 due to his age), for spending close to double the legal limit during his failed attempt to win re-election in 2012.

The case was known as the Bygmalion affair, after the name of the public relations firm hired by Sarkozy to orchestrate a blitz of lavish US-style election rallies. Executives of the firm admitted to using a system of fake invoices to mask the real cost of the events.

Instead, French candidates receive free, allocated public airtime, where they promote their campaign message.

Other prohibited expenses in France include campaign bills paid directly by the candidate, a supporter or a third party; personal expenses such as clothing, medical care, cosmetics, or private living costs; parking tickets and tax penalties; and lavish private social receptions unrelated to public election meetings.

The biggest spenders usually win

Historical examples suggest that spending up to the maximum is worth it.

Emmanuel Macron beat Marine Le Pen in the second round of the 2022 presidential election, after outspending her by roughly €6.03 million - a repeat of what happened in the 2017 presidential election, when he spent €4 million more than her. 

Nicolas Sarkozy won the 2007 presidential election after outspending his rivals and Chirac won the 1995 and 2002 elections as the biggest spender.

One recent exception is the 2012 election in which Nicolas Sarkozy lost to François Hollande in the second round despite spending more money. That year, Sarkozy didn't receive any reimbursement from the state to cover campaign costs after breaching the spending limit. He was officially left with close to €23 million to cover himself.

Campaign accounts are centralised and monitored

Candidates are not allowed to directly collect donations or pay campaign expenses. Instead, all candidates on the official list must declare a campaign account, which is managed by a financial agent, which can be an individual or an electoral financing association.

This account details income, expenses, in-kind contributions, supporting documents (including invoices and examples of campaign materials such as leaflets), and transactions in the agent's bank account.

The Commission nationale des comptes de campagne et des financements politiques (CNCCFP) monitors the campaign accounts and political financing of candidates in French elections. 

Those who break the rules face heavy (albeit often delayed) penalties

If the CNCCFP finds irregularities in a candidate's campaign accounts, it can ask judicial authorities to launch an investigation.

The most famous example of someone who has fallen foul of this system is former president Nicolas Sarkozy.

In 2021, a court sentenced Sarkozy to one year in prison (later reduced to six months with an electronic tag, which a judge waived in May 2026 due to his age), for spending close to double the legal limit during his failed attempt to win re-election in 2012.

The case was known as the Bygmalion affair, after the name of the public relations firm hired by Sarkozy to orchestrate a blitz of lavish US-style election rallies. Executives of the firm admitted to using a system of fake invoices to mask the real cost of the events.
