news.title: My Turn: Tax the rich. Fund public education. Win elections.
news.text:
One of Wallace Steven’s most famous poems is “Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird.” I’ve come back repeatedly to the fifth stanza:

I do not know which to prefer,The beauty of inflectionsOr the beauty of innuendoes,The blackbird whistlingOr just after. 

We just had an election of monumental importance. And now the stories get told about what it meant. The election was the “inflection.” What we make of it is the “innuendo.”

The poet insists he does “not know which to prefer.” In politics, we have no choice but to look forward, to tell the story and to shape the “innuendoes.”

One key lesson from the beautifully unexpected repudiation of President Donald Trump and his lapdog enablers in the Party of Trump and in the billionaire class is that fighting to retake the country from the wealthy in order to fund public education, a core common good, is a recipe for electoral victory.

Look at the shocking victories in Texas. Gina Hinojosa, who will be the first Latina governor in the history of Texas, was inspired to run, and made as a foundation of her campaign, the fight for public schools. She beat Gov. Greg Abbott, who was seen as unbeatable only days before the election. James Talarico was a public school teacher who built his reputation in the Texas legislature as a defender of public education and became an outspoken opponent of Abbott and the Republican Party’s decimation of public education through private school vouchers and public school funding cuts. 

Dozens of other candidates in states across the country made investing in public education— and protecting it from private school voucher schemes that are designed to crush the very idea of universal, free, public education — a key plank. The Prop 3 referendum to make permanent a tax on millionaires to fund public education passed almost 60-40 in California. Meanwhile, the Prop 40 California wealth tax, which was focused on protecting healthcare, was opposed by the $300 million of a few billionaires, suffered from a lack of funds and division in the labor coalition, and ultimately failed.

Washington voters soundly rejected an attempt by the very rich to roll back the millionaire’s tax, modeled on our own Fair Share Amendment, which will benefit public education. Here in Massachusetts, we rejected the second of two attempts to undermine the Fair Share Amendment, the 2024 amendment to our Constitution that is bringing in over $3 billion a year from the wealthiest residents of the commonwealth. Those efforts were led by the Mass High Tech Council, Pioneer Institute and Competitiveness Council. They resent that we, the citizens of Massachusetts, are “calling back,” in the words of our Amherst permanent poet laureate, Emily Dickinson, about $3 billion a year to fund everything from more childcare, to universal school meals, to free higher education and better roads and bridges and public transportation. One of those efforts was thrown out by the Supreme Judicial Court, the other by the voters on Nov. 3.

And this is hardly new. Look back to the 2024 election. In Kentucky, Trump beat Kamala Harris by 30 points. But those same voters, on the same ballot, voted by the exact same margin to reject private school vouchers. In Nebraska, where Trump won about 60% of the vote, vouchers were rejected 57-42. You can’t achieve that result unless many of the voters who voted to return Trump to the White House also rejected one of his and the Republicans’ central — and maybe their only — public education policy: diverting public money to private and religious schools. 

When I was president of the Massachusetts Teachers Association and traveling almost daily up to Gloucester during the educator strike (which was illegal in Massachusetts, incidentally) in November 2024, I was struck by a house at the bottom of the off-ramp from Route 1. On one column of the front porch was a MAGA “Make America Great Again” sign. And on the other column was a sign with this message: “Support the Union of Gloucester Educators.” People can gravitate toward conservative candidates who appear populist, but they care deeply about the public schools and public school educators to which they entrust their children. 

And they want to tax the very rich, to take back some of their ungodly power to purchase elected officials and policies that benefit the rich and to invest in the things voters care about, most centrally public education. A recent poll by Hart Research, which was commissioned by Better Taxes for a Better America, found that 85% of voters felt that the wealthy should be taxed more. That number beat out the response to questions about whether or not the Earth is round and if apple pie is tasty. In other words, we have a near-universal consensus that the wealthy need to pay their fair share, as long as the money is invested in what matters most, and public education is at the top of the list. 

We are at an inflection point. Let the “innuendoes” from this election make their way into the public policy platforms of 2028 and beyond.

Max Page is a professor of architecture at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

news.title: 'I'm Not Gay': GOP Rep.-Elect Launches Campaign To 'Get Every Gay American To Be Republican'
news.text:
Rep.-elect Anthony Constantino (R-N.Y.) bizarrely shared purported thirsty messages from “gay Americans” as proof that his drive to recruit them to the Republican Party is working.

“It’s already begun,” he wrote Monday on X. “I want to clarify, I am not Gay but I do want all Gay Americans to become Republican. The Democrat Party is making it unsafe to be Gay. If you like Secure Borders, Safety, Low Taxes, Less Regulation, as well as First and Second Amendment Rights then you should be Republican.”

“You turned me Republican,” one comment read. “Sexy, let me know if you want to play,” went another.

Constantino, who is replacing Elise Stefanik in the upstate district, also targeted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani in an Islamophobic rant that baselessly claimed Mamdani had “conned Gays.”

“It makes no sense that any Gay American wants to be in the Party of Mamdani,” he wrote. “These Muslims are LAUGHING AT YOU. They think Gays are stupid for voting for Democrats. This is all Zohran talks about when he goes to Uganda. He giggles like Hyena about the FACT that he conned Gays.”

HuffPost has reached out to Mamdani’s office for comment.

Constantino said in a short video on Sunday his goal was to “get every gay American to be Republican. More on this soon.”

He followed with a similar pledge Monday ― again without details of his supposed outreach.

“Hey American, everybody wants to know how I’m gonna turn every gay American Republican. It’s easy. Watch,” he began.

Constantino then did a bit of in-car karaoke to Stevie Wonder’s 1980 song “Master Blaster (Jammin’).”

“We’ve agreed to get together, joined as children in Jah,” the incoming lawmaker sang in his X post. “When you’re moving in the positive, your destination is the brightest star.” 

Constantino will have his work cut out for him. Within the blue wave that crushed Republicans in the midterm was a Democratic rainbow wave of LGBTQ+ winners, led by Sen.-elect Chris Pappas (N.H.).

As for the electorate: Even amid President Donald Trump’s victory in 2024, Democrat Kamala Harris still dominated him 86% to 12% among LGBTQ voters, NBC reported.

news.title: New York congressman-elect on crusade to make gay Americans Republican
news.text:
Representative-elect Anthony Constantino of New York says he wants to persuade gay Americans to join the Republican Party. The incoming congressman, whose first posts about the effort drew flirtatious messages on social media, has since clarified that he is not gay while continuing to promote his political appeal.

In a video posted to X on November 21, Constantino said: “Now that I’m elected, one of my big goals is to get every gay American to be Republican.” He did not provide details in the video but promised to say more about the effort soon.

Constantino later shared what appeared to be screenshots of private messages, with the senders’ names obscured. Some were flirtatious, with one saying, “You turned me republican.” Constantino posted publicly in response, “I am not Gay but I do want all Gay Americans to become Republican.”

Constantino continued: “The Democrat Party is making it unsafe to be Gay. If you like Secure Borders, Safety, Low Taxes, Less Regulation, as well as First and Second Amendment Rights then you should be Republican.”

In a statement to Newsweek, Jeremy Comeau, the president of the National Federation of Stonewall Democrats, said: “As for the claim that Democrats are making it unsafe to be gay, LGBTQ people know exactly who has been writing the laws aimed at us, and it isn’t Democrats. Republicans have spent years passing bills that target transgender Americans, pushing to roll back marriage equality, and turning our lives into campaign attack ads. You don’t get to light the fire and then sell us the extinguisher.

“The data isn’t close. LGBTQ voters backed Democrats by 86 percent in this month’s exit polls. That isn’t blind party loyalty. It’s a reaction to what Republicans have actually done. If Republicans truly want to earn gay votes, the path is simple. Stop legislating against trans people. Put marriage equality protections into law and keep them there. Support the Equality Act. Protect funding for HIV prevention and care. Until that happens, no post from a congressman-elect is going to change the math.”

Comeau’s 86 percent figure matches reported 2024 presidential exit-poll results for LGBTQ voters. According to ABC News’ 2026 House voter poll, 87 percent of respondents who identified as gay, lesbian, bisexual or transgender said they voted for a Democratic House candidate, while 12 percent said they voted Republican.

In a New York Post interview, Constantino argued that Democrats “are against the gay community,” and that high-income and hardworking gay voters align better with Republican values around taxes, regulation, border security and gun rights. 

Newsweek has contacted Constantino’s campaign for comment via email outside regular office hours.

Constantino is set to take office in January after narrowly defeating Democrat Blake Gendebien in the 21st Congressional District, a large, mostly rural area in northern and central New York.

The 44-year-old founder of the printing company Sticker Mule and supporter of President Donald Trump faces early friction from local GOP officials, such as Plattsburgh Republican Chair David J. Souliere IV, who urged him to focus on local affordability and health care rather than online rhetoric.

What Constantino Says He Wants to Change

Constantino’s post sets out an initial argument for why gay Americans should support Republicans: a list of priorities that includes taxes, regulation, border security and gun rights.

He has not yet described a campaign or outreach plan, or explained how he would address policy questions that have historically shaped LGBTQ voters’ views of the parties.

How LGBTQ Americans Have Voted

Recent voting data shows the challenge Constantino faces as he works to recruit gay voters to his party. In 2024, NBC’s national exit poll found that 86 percent of LGBTQ voters backed the Democratic candidate, then-Vice President Kamala Harris, while 12 percent backed Trump. 

Exit polling has also shown movement between elections. The same polling series found that Democrat Joe Biden received 64 percent of the LGBTQ vote in 2020, compared with 27 percent for Trump. Those figures describe LGBTQ voters as a group, not gay men alone, and exit polls are estimates rather than a count of every voter.

Survey data on party identity point in a similar direction. A Pew Research Center survey conducted in January 2025 found that 80 percent of LGBTQ adults identified with or leaned toward the Democratic Party, compared with 16 percent who identified with or leaned Republican. The survey was conducted before Trump issued several executive orders related to transgender rights at the beginning of his second term.

Pew also found differences among LGBTQ Republicans and Democrats in how they viewed the parties’ approach to the community. Twenty-four percent of LGBTQ Republicans said the Republican Party was friendly toward gay, lesbian or bisexual people, while 63 percent of LGBTQ Democrats said the same of the Democratic Party. Those views were less favorable when respondents were asked about transgender people.

The Republican Party’s LGBTQ Outreach

Constantino’s pitch also lands amid debate within the Republican Party about its relationship with LGBTQ voters. Log Cabin Republicans is a national organization that promotes Republican candidates and policies to LGBTQ voters. In an August essay, the group’s president, Ross Hemminger, said the organization would refocus its advocacy on lesbian, gay and bisexual issues, ending its advocacy for trans rights.

Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Shakeema Edwards.

WSJ: Jensen Huang’s return as the leather-clad philanderer-in-chief at Nvidia has saved the stock market. What could possibly go wrong?

On Monday the Nasdaq was up 7% as Nvidia added $1 trillion to its market value, and more than four in five members of the S&P 500 were up. Forget worries about the AI bubble; focus on support from the U.S. president for a company that’s still, it claims, carrying out an independent investigation into its former-and-new CEO’s entanglement with an alleged Chinese spy.

The question is whether the market reaction will turn out to be an epic version of what traders call a dead cat bounce, when a plunging market temporarily rebounds.

Traders focused on the short term, and in the short term it’s all good.

Ed: Well, given my decision to retire at the start of the new year, it's all good for me too. I must admit that the stock market rebound was music to my ears. However, this raises all sorts of questions about the intersection of Big Tech and government, not to mention whether Huang got a free pass out of a honeypot operation that may have damaged our national security position on the basis of Who You Know.

There may be a legitimate reason for a pardon if Huang truly didn't do anything wrong, or if he completely cooperated in dealing with an intelligence op aimed at our AI sector. Semafor: The decision to grant Huang a second act will only strengthen the unchecked powers of the “imperial CEO,” and confirms the Trump administration’s readiness to treat corporate America as an instrument of presidential power.

The most important line in the company’s 465-word announcement was the one saying that “input from senior levels of the United States government” had reassured the board that Huang’s return would pose no national security risk. Even before Semafor reported that US President Donald Trump had dialed into Nvidia’s board meeting, the statement left little doubt as to where that input had come from. On Sunday, Trump posted on social media that rehiring Huang would be “the best thing for the Company, and also, for the USA.”

Nvidia’s uncommonly long-serving board was facing enough pressure even before this intervention: The company’s stock had fallen 40% in a month, erasing $2 trillion of market value and unleashing a chorus of calls from investors, employees, and customers for Huang’s return.

The chip giant’s directors found themselves in this position because they failed in their duty to develop a credible replacement for a co-founder who became Nvidia’s indispensable chief salesman, chief technologist, and chief diplomat. Its belated steps — investigations, committees, executive searches — do little to suggest that the events of the past two weeks have taught Nvidia’s directors much about the importance of succession planning or corporate governance checks and balances.

Tara Palmeri: On Saturday afternoon, I found myself seated at John’s Grill, the century-old San Francisco watering-hole for politicians and celebrities next to the man who had more to do with the careers of 2028 frontrunners Kamala Harris and Gavin Newsom than anyone else: Willie Brown.

Brown grew up a shoeshine boy and field hand in Jim Crow Texas, in a town with frequent white-on-Black violence. He became a sought-after attorney and the most influential power broker in California, first as Speaker of the Assembly and then as mayor of San Francisco, and a political godfather to Harris and Newsom.

Jim Geraghty at NRO: But even if we unrealistically assume all 32 million copies of GTA VI were sold in the United States, and everyone spent the past few days playing the game . . . we’re a country of roughly 343 million people now. One reason GTA VI is unlikely to ever be as popular as those other examples is that it isn’t made to appeal to everyone. But if you adjust for inflation, Box Office Mojo calculates that The Ten Commandments sold 131 million tickets, E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial sold 141 million, The Sound of Music sold 142 million, the original Star Wars in 1977 sold 178 million, and Gone with the Wind sold 200 million tickets. (Those figures are worldwide, but keep in mind that in the past, overseas ticket sales were a much smaller proportion of the total sales.)

The point is not that this movie is better than that movie, but to observe that in the past, a hit movie could have a bigger cultural impact because it permeated a wider swath and a greater proportion of the total population.

That is probably the right outcome. In the wake of his departure, it was already clear that the board had acted too hastily. For all the allegations thrown around, it was far from clear that Huang was really guilty of anything other than breaking his marriage vows. It was not proved that his Chinese mistress, Alice Huang (no relation), was really a “honeypot agent” of the Chinese government, while the second affair, this one with a senior Nvidia executive, may have broken company rules, but was completely consensual. Huang may have acted foolishly. But he had also built Nvidia from nothing and turned it into the world’s largest company, as well as the driving force behind America’s huge global lead in AI. Given that none of the other potential candidates, either internal or external, had anything like the same level of knowledge or ability, bringing him back was the only realistic option. Even worse, an open civil war would have crippled the business. 

In the wake of the CEO’s return, two points are now clear. To start with, Huang will be more powerful than ever. He may only own 4 percent of the stock, but he has just proved how completely indispensable he is to its future. The Nvidians who didn’t sign the “Stand With Jensen” petition must be feeling, to put it mildly, a little uncomfortable by now, while the position of the board, after making such a mess of the whole process, is surely untenable. The chairman Harvey C. Jones will have to be replaced, and so will most of the other non-executives. Within the company, Huang’s authority will be total. 

And, more importantly, his restoration is a victory for visionary leaders over the dead hand of a few box-ticking, DEI-obsessed corporate functionaries. In reality, leaders of Huang’s fierce intelligence, drive and ambition, are all too rare. In global business, only Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg and possibly Anthropic’s Dario Amodei come anywhere close to his level of ability. You can’t change the world by committee, nor can you build a whole new world-changing industry while obsessing over whether all the HR guidelines have been followed. Corporate America has been dialing down the fixation on DEI and political correctness over the last two years. But Huang’s victory over the Nvidia board will confirm it. In the end, ability is what matters more than anything else.

news.title: James Carville warns Gavin Newsom faces California baggage in potential 2028 run
news.text: Democratic strategist James Carville suggested that California Gov. Gavin Newsom will have to reckon with Americans weary of liberal coastal politics if he runs in 2028. Speaking on the Politicon podcast with political adviser Mark McKinnon Friday, Carville weighed in on potential contenders for the 2028 Democratic nomination. When asked about Newsom’s chances, he argued that one key issue stands in his way. "Well, his strength is he runs the biggest state. He's got a huge fundraising base. There's no doubt about it. If you’re the governor of California, you could raise a lot of money," Carville said. "His problem is, ‘Are we going to do this California sh-- again? Really? Is that what we're going to do?’" "He's got to overcome that kind of barrier," Carville warned, suggesting many voters are wary of an "uber coastal candidate" leading the country. NEWSOM ROASTED ONLINE FOR 'STAGED' FLY-FISHING INTERVIEW WITH CNN ANCHOR WHERE HE DROPPED MAJOR 2028 HINT McKinnon said he was initially skeptical that Newsom might be "a little too slick, a little too Hollywood," but was impressed after interviewing him several times on his own podcast. "I mean, he's got chops," McKinnon said. Carville agreed that Newsom is quick on his feet and possesses real political skill, noting that navigating California's Democratic politics is far more difficult than outsiders assume. He also credited Newsom for being authentic to his roots, comparing the governor's California persona to his own Louisiana identity. NEWSOM ADMITS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST IDEAS ‘MAINSTREAM’ IN DEMOCRAT PARTY: ‘PRETTY ALIGNED’ "To his credit, he's a real California guy," he said. "He don't try to fake it." Other party insiders remain skeptical of Newsom's national appeal. Veteran Democratic strategist Doug Schoen suggested that "Gavin Newsom has no clear identity. Some days he's a moderate Bill Clinton type and on other days he tries to be a progressive — for example, he's for a national wealth tax, and he has recently commuted the sentences of hundreds of death row inmates." "His weaknesses are that he has no clear message or strategy, and that he goes whichever way the wind blows." Still, Schoen acknowledged Newsom is a serious contender because of his fundraising power and home-state base. Although Newsom has previously said he would not run if former Vice President Kamala Harris enters the race, Schoen said the governor appears eager to launch a campaign of his own. "This seems like a warning shot towards Kamala, as there is every indication that he's chomping at the bit to run himself."
news.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville says Gavin Newsom faces a major 2028 hurdle in that voters are weary of "California" style coastal politics.
